metadata.title: Kronig-Penney Band Gap Explorer — Two Panels, One Missing Bridge

beats.narration_text: Ciao. This is Liam, in for Bear. We asked Claude for a Kronig-Penney band structure explorer — two D3 panels, two sliders, live physics checks. Today we judge the visualization, not the physics it teaches.

props.command: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for the Kronig-Penney band model.
output: ✓ D3.js from CDN — no build step
✓ two panels: KP function + reduced-zone bands

beats.narration_text: The sim opens on two D3 panels. Left: the KP function f of qa plotted against qa from zero to four pi — a red curve, pale red shading where the curve escapes the dashed plus-one minus-one corridor. Right: the reduced-zone band structure — energy in electron-volts against the Bloch wavevector, normalized to pi over a. Red band curves. A gray dashed free-electron parabola. Horizontal gap shading. Sidebar: two sliders for the barrier strength P and the lattice constant a, a live Band Info panel with gap width and center in eV, and three Physics Check icons.

P is the barrier strength slider — it runs from zero to twenty. Sweep it from three to twenty. On the left, the f-of-qa oscillation grows: more of the red curve escapes the plus-minus-one corridor. On the right, the gap shading expands — bands compress, gaps widen. At P equals twenty, the model is approaching the tight-binding limit, where electrons are nearly localized to individual wells. The two panels update together. That simultaneous update is the visualization's argument.

Three things the visualization gets right. First: the two-panel layout. Left panel shows the constraint — where f of qa escapes the corridor, no Bloch state can exist. Right panel shows the consequence — energy gaps. This is the KP argument made geometric. Second: the plus-minus-one dashed lines. The allowed-forbidden threshold is drawn as a literal corridor the curve must stay inside. No memorization required. Third: the free-electron parabola stays visible throughout as gray dashes. As P grows, the student watches the real bands diverge from the parabola — building intuition for what periodic potential does to a free electron.

Three things the visualization hides. First: P is dimensionless — P equals mV-zero times b times a over h-bar squared — but the slider just shows three-point-zero. No formula. No example material. Students move a magic knob. Second: there is no visual bridge between the two panels. Both panels update together, but nothing links a specific escape in the f-of-qa curve to the corresponding gap in band structure. That connection is the entire argument, and the viz leaves students to infer it. Third: the Physics Checks use three states — check, cross, and circle — and never explain that circle means inactive. At the default settings, all three show circle. Students cannot tell whether those conditions passed, failed, or were never tested.

Let's recap with Claude. The two-panel layout is the correct pedagogical move — it makes the KP constraint and its consequence visible at the same time. But the P slider needs a formula, and the two panels need a visual link. Use this sim after deriving the band gaps analytically, not before — the visualization confirms and explores; it does not discover. The one fix that matters most: one connector line, from a selected point on the f-of-qa curve into the corresponding energy on the band structure. That bridge would complete the argument.

artifactLines: Two synchronized panels — the constraint and its consequence shown at once.
P = magic knob. No formula, no material, no units.
Panels update together — but no visual bridge connects them.
Use it AFTER deriving the gaps, not to discover them.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt: I have a Kronig-Penney Band Gap Explorer. Fix two things. One: the P slider shows a bare number. Add an annotation showing P equals mV-zero times b times a over h-bar squared — dimensionless — and map P equals three to a realistic material, such as a GaAs-AlGaAs-style barrier. Two: add a click interaction. When a user clicks a point on the f-of-qa curve, draw a horizontal dashed line to the corresponding energy in the band structure panel. Keep the single-file D3 format. End prompt. The formula annotation gives the slider physical meaning. The connector line completes the argument. Two edits — two missing things found. Run this in your session.

props.command: I have a Kronig-Penney Band Gap Explorer. Fix two things. (1) P slider shows a bare number — add an annotation showing P = mV₀ba/ħ² (dimensionless) and map P=3 to a realistic material (e.g., GaAs/AlGaAs-style barrier). (2) Add a click interaction: when a user clicks a point on the f(qa) curve, draw a horizontal dashed line to the corresponding energy in the band structure panel. Keep the single-file D3 format.
